entities.summary:
Natalis, Archbishop of Milan (c. 740–747 CE), emerged as a significant ecclesiastical figure in Lombard Italy during a tumultuous period marked by the decline of Byzantine influence and the rise of the Carolingian Franks. He is venerated as a saint in both Eastern Orthodox and Roman Catholic traditions, underscoring his spiritual authority and the enduring impact of his episcopacy. His tenure coincided with critical shifts in Italian political and religious power dynamics, particularly the increasing independence of the Lombard kingdom from Constantinople and the burgeoning temporal ambitions of the Papacy, all while navigating the complex interplay of secular and spiritual power in the early medieval West.

During his archiepiscopate, Natalis likely focused on consolidating the spiritual and administrative authority of the Milanese see, a crucial metropolitan center in northern Italy. While specific details of his actions are scarce, his leadership would have been instrumental in navigating the complex relationship between the local Lombard rulers, the fading Byzantine exarchate in Ravenna, and the nascent Frankish power. Milan, as a former capital of the Western Roman Empire, held immense symbolic weight, and Natalis would have overseen its spiritual life, including liturgical practices and monastic foundations, against a backdrop of ongoing theological disputes and barbarian incursions.
